Quick answer: Arthritis risk rises with age due to cartilage changes, muscle loss and conditions like polymyalgia rheumatica and gout becoming more common — but it is not inevitable. Treatment often needs extra care around kidney/liver function and drug interactions, and joint pain is closely linked to falls risk, making strength and balance exercise a genuinely protective measure.

Arthritis and Ageing: What Actually Changes

Arthritis becomes more common as we get older, but it isn't an inevitable part of ageing that everyone must simply accept. Understanding what genuinely changes with age — and what doesn't — makes it easier to manage joint health well into later life rather than assuming pain is just "part of getting old."

Cartilage naturally becomes slightly less resilient with age, joints lose some of their range of motion, and muscle mass tends to decline unless it's actively maintained — all of which raise the risk of osteoarthritis and make joint pain more noticeable. Conditions such as polymyalgia rheumatica, which almost exclusively affects people over 50, and gout, which becomes more common with age, are also more relevant in later life. But plenty of older adults have strong, comfortable joints well into their 80s and 90s — age alone doesn't guarantee arthritis, and lifestyle factors continue to matter throughout life.

Conditions More Common in Older Adults

  • Osteoarthritis — the most common form overall, and its prevalence rises steadily with age as cartilage wear accumulates.
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) — causes stiffness and aching in the shoulders, neck and hips, almost always in people over 50, and responds well to low-dose steroid treatment.
  • Gout — becomes more common with age, partly due to increasing use of medications (like some blood pressure treatments) that raise uric acid levels.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — can develop at any age but a second peak in new diagnoses occurs in later life.

Why Diagnosis Can Be Trickier in Older Adults

Joint pain in later life is sometimes dismissed — by patients and, occasionally, by services — as an unavoidable consequence of ageing, which can delay proper diagnosis and treatment. Older adults are also more likely to have several health conditions at once, which can mask or mimic arthritis symptoms, and some blood markers used to help diagnose inflammatory arthritis can behave differently with age. It's worth being persistent: new or worsening joint pain, especially with stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes each morning, is always worth raising with a GP rather than assuming nothing can be done.

Medication Considerations Specific to Older Adults

Treating arthritis in older adults often requires extra care around medication choices:

  • NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) carry higher risks of stomach, kidney and cardiovascular side effects in older adults, particularly alongside other common medications such as blood pressure tablets or blood thinners. GPs often recommend topical NSAID gels over oral tablets where possible, or the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time.
  • Kidney and liver function naturally decline somewhat with age, which affects how the body processes many arthritis medications — doses may need adjusting, and blood tests to monitor organ function are more frequently used.
  • Polypharmacy — taking several medications for different conditions — increases the risk of drug interactions, so it's worth a pharmacist or GP periodically reviewing your full medication list together.
  • Steroid treatment for conditions like PMR is very effective but requires monitoring for bone density (osteoporosis risk) and blood sugar, both of particular relevance in later life.

None of this means older adults can't be treated effectively — it means treatment plans are usually more individualised, with closer monitoring built in.

Mobility, Falls and Independence

One of the most important, and most under-discussed, aspects of arthritis in older adults is its link to falls risk and long-term independence. Painful or stiff joints change the way people walk, often unconsciously, which affects balance. Weak muscles around an arthritic joint — particularly the knee or hip — reduce the body's ability to catch a stumble before it becomes a fall. This matters because falls are a leading cause of injury and loss of independence in older adults.

The encouraging part: this is one of the most modifiable risk factors in arthritis care. Regular strength and balance work — even simple, seated or supported exercises — measurably improves stability and confidence in walking, and physiotherapists can tailor a programme to whatever level of mobility someone currently has.

Staying Active Safely

  • Low-impact exercise — walking, swimming, water aerobics and cycling — puts less strain on joints than high-impact activity while still building the strength and cardiovascular fitness that protect against falls and frailty.
  • Strength training, even with light resistance bands or bodyweight, helps counter the natural muscle loss (sarcopenia) that compounds joint problems with age.
  • Balance exercises, such as tai chi, have good evidence behind them specifically for reducing falls risk in older adults with joint conditions.
  • Pacing and rest remain important — the goal is consistent, manageable activity, not pushing through pain, especially during a flare of an inflammatory condition like PMR.

Always check with a GP or physiotherapist before starting a new exercise routine if you have other health conditions alongside arthritis, so the plan can be tailored safely.

Nutrition and Bone Health

Diet plays a supporting role in joint health at any age, but a few things become particularly relevant in later life. Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake matter more as bone density naturally declines with age, and this becomes especially important for anyone on long-term steroid treatment (such as for PMR), which can further reduce bone density over time — bone density scans (DEXA scans) are often recommended periodically in this situation. Maintaining sufficient protein intake helps counter age-related muscle loss, working alongside strength exercise rather than replacing it. And for gout specifically, dietary triggers such as excess alcohol, red meat and sugary drinks become worth managing more actively, since gout risk increases with age.

None of this requires a dramatically different diet from general healthy-eating advice — it's more a case of paying closer attention to a few specific nutrients that matter more as the body changes with age.

Getting the Right Support

Later life often comes with access to services specifically geared toward joint health and independence that are worth knowing about: falls-prevention clinics, community physiotherapy services, occupational therapy assessments for home adaptations, and social prescribing schemes that can connect people to local exercise groups or peer support. A GP or local Age UK service can point toward what's available in your area — many people aren't aware how much support exists until they ask.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is joint pain just a normal part of getting older? Some increase in joint stiffness is common with age, but persistent pain, swelling, or stiffness lasting over 30 minutes each morning is not something to simply accept — it's worth discussing with a GP, since effective treatments exist regardless of age.

Are older adults less able to have joint replacement surgery? Age alone is rarely a barrier — overall health and fitness for surgery matter far more than age itself, and many people have successful joint replacements well into their 80s.

Why does polymyalgia rheumatica mainly affect older people? It's not fully understood why PMR is so strongly age-related, but it's rare under 50 and most commonly diagnosed in people over 70, likely reflecting age-related changes in immune function.

Can exercise make arthritis worse in older adults? Appropriately paced, low-impact exercise generally improves arthritis symptoms rather than worsening them. The main risk is doing too much too quickly rather than exercise itself — building up gradually is key.

Key Takeaways

  • Arthritis risk increases with age, but it isn't an unavoidable consequence of ageing, and effective treatment is available at any age.
  • Conditions like polymyalgia rheumatica and gout become more relevant in later life alongside the more familiar osteoarthritis.
  • Medication choices often need extra care in older adults due to kidney/liver changes and interactions with other medicines.
  • Joint pain is closely linked to falls risk in older adults, making strength and balance work a genuinely protective, not just comfort-focused, intervention.
  • Persistent joint symptoms are always worth raising with a GP, regardless of age.

This article provides general information and is not a substitute for personalised medical advice. Speak to your GP about any new or worsening joint symptoms.
